title: Where you go
hookLine: Ruth to Naomi: where you go I will go

cards: Three widows are standing on a road out of Moab. Naomi, the older one, has buried her husband and both her sons. Her two daughters-in-law, Orpah and Ruth, have buried their husbands too.
Naomi is heading home to Bethlehem, and she tells the young women to turn around: "Go, return each to her mother's house." She has nothing left to give them. They cry.
Orpah kisses her and goes. Ruth doesn't move. The King James puts it in a handful of words: "Ruth clave unto her."

teach.h: ORPAH GOES, AND NO ONE BLAMES HER.
teach.b: Start with the one who leaves, because the story is kind to her. Naomi asked both women to go, and blessed them: "the LORD deal kindly with you, as ye have dealt with the dead, and with me."
Orpah does what she was asked, and the text never scolds her. Going home was sensible, and allowed. That's what makes Ruth stand out: she had an honorable way out, and didn't take it.

"Ruth clave unto her" uses the same English verb the King James uses in Genesis for a man who will "cleave unto his wife." Clinging, holding on. Earlier this year came her opening words, whither thou goest.

teach.h: WHERE THOU DIEST, WILL I DIE.
teach.b: Today, the line that follows, which goes further: "Where thou diest, will I die, and there will I be buried." Ruth isn't promising a trip.
She's promising a whole life, and a grave, in a country where she'll be the foreigner: yesterday's stranger, seen from the other side. She doesn't talk about how she feels; she names a direction.
In Bethlehem, Ruth gleans, gathering leftover barley behind the reapers in someone else's field so the two of them can eat.
Later the field's owner, Boaz, tells her: "thou hast shewed more kindness in the latter end than at the beginning."
The Hebrew behind kindness there is chesed, the steady, loyal love from the start of this block.
Some readers take that sentence as the book's quiet center: love that keeps going after the moment when leaving would have been fine.

how: Ruth's words to Naomi are read at some weddings and conversion ceremonies, and in Jewish communities the book of Ruth is read at the festival of Shavuot.

games.q: you're Naomi. two young widows are walking with you toward a country where you have nothing to give them. what do you do?
o: say nothing and let them come.
send them home, with a blessing.
make them promise never to leave.
games.why: Naomi sends them back and blesses them: the LORD deal kindly with you. Orpah goes, and the text doesn't blame her. Ruth clings, and stays.

practice: Let one person come to mind who is in a hard stretch, someone it would be easy, even reasonable, to drift away from, and picture walking beside them one more mile.

You're not fixing anything, just staying; if you pray, you can hold them before God by name. Then let a quiet question rest there: what would staying look like, a call, a ride, an hour on their couch?

wordCard.voice: Ruth. The widow who left her own people to stay with Naomi, and gleaned barley in Bethlehem so the two of them could eat. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: steady, loyal love; the word behind kindness when Boaz praises Ruth.

carryVoice: Your line: clinging, holding on. A promise with a direction in it. Day eight hundred twenty-seven, done.
